title: Formal exponential factorization for elements with central pairwise brackets
statement:
Let $A$ be any associative unital $\mathbf Q$-algebra, not assumed commutative. Write $A[[s,t]]$ for formal power series in central commuting indeterminates, with coefficientwise addition and Cauchy multiplication. For a series $Z$ with zero constant coefficient set $\exp(Z)=\sum_{n\geq0}Z^n/n!$; each coefficient is a finite sum. Fix $r\geq0$ and $Z_1,\ldots,Z_r\in(s,t)A[[s,t]]$. Use the commutator Lie algebra [def-wf-lie-algebra] on this associative algebra of series, with $[X,Y]=XY-YX$ (the alternating and Jacobi identities follow by expanding products). Assume $[[Z_i,Z_j],Z_k]=0$ for every $1\leq i,j,k\leq r$. Then
$$\exp\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^rZ_i\right)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^r\exp(Z_i)\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac12\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq r}[Z_i,Z_j]\right),$$
where the product is in increasing index order. This includes $r=0$, with empty sum zero and empty product one.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivates formal root exponentials but does not state this identity. Agent-stated class-two formal exponential identity. WANTED: Bourbaki, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Chapter II, Campbell--Hausdorff series, its central-bracket specialization.

proof.text: Put $B=A[[s,t]]$, $X_i=Z_i$, $S=\sum_iX_i$, $C_{ij}=X_iX_j-X_jX_i$ and $C=\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}$. All sums over $i$ below run from $1$ to $r$. The bracket notation is that of [def-wf-lie-algebra]; we use its associative commutator example, with the bracket explicitly specified in the item. The hypothesis says precisely $C_{ij}X_k=X_kC_{ij}$. Thus $C$ commutes with every $X_k$, and consequently with every power of $X_k$ and with every coefficient of the series $E_k$ defined next: the power assertion follows by induction, and the coefficient assertion by rational linearity. We do not assume these commutators commute with all of $B$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivation only; agent-supplied formal coefficient argument: notation and the exact consequence of the triple-bracket hypothesis

proof.text:
Adjoin one more central variable $u$ and work in $B[[u]]$. Define
$$E_i(u)=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{u^nX_i^n}{n!},\qquad E_S(u)=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{u^nS^n}{n!},\qquad Q(u)=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{u^{2n}(-C/2)^n}{n!}.$$
These are well-defined series in $u$, without evaluating $u$ anywhere. Write $D(\sum a_nu^n)=\sum(n+1)a_{n+1}u^n$. This operator is additive and obeys $D(FG)=(DF)G+F(DG)$ even though $B$ need not be commutative: at degree $n$, the two sums on the right contain $a_p b_q$ with $p+q=n+1$, weighted respectively by $p$ and $q$ (the boundary terms of weight zero may be inserted); their sum is $(n+1)\sum_{p+q=n+1}a_p b_q$, the coefficient on the left. The order $a_p b_q$ never changes.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivation only; agent-supplied formal coefficient argument: the auxiliary variable and a direct finite-sum proof of the noncommutative product rule

proof.text:
The defining coefficients give $DE_i=X_iE_i$ and $DE_S=SE_S$: at degree $n$, $(n+1)X_i^{n+1}/(n+1)!=X_iX_i^n/n!$, and the same calculation applies to $S$. Also $DQ=-uCQ$. Indeed both sides have zero coefficients in even degrees, and at degree $2n-1$ for $n\geq1$ the required equality is
$$\frac{2n(-C/2)^n}{n!}=-C\,\frac{(-C/2)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}.$$
Every $E_i$, $E_S$ and $Q$ has constant coefficient $1$. By step 1, $C$ commutes coefficientwise with each $E_i$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivation only; agent-supplied formal coefficient argument: coefficient computations of the three derivatives and initial values

proof.text:
For $i<j$ we claim
$$X_i^nX_j=X_jX_i^n+nC_{ij}X_i^{n-1}\quad(n\geq1).$$
At $n=1$ this is the definition of $C_{ij}$. If it holds at $n$, multiplication on the left by $X_i$, followed by $X_iX_j=X_jX_i+C_{ij}$ and $X_iC_{ij}=C_{ij}X_i$, gives
$$X_i^{n+1}X_j=X_jX_i^{n+1}+C_{ij}X_i^n+nC_{ij}X_i^n.$$
This proves the induction. Compare coefficients of $u^n$ and divide by $n!$; at $n=0$ both sides are $X_j$. We obtain
$$E_iX_j=(X_j+uC_{ij})E_i.$$
Here the shifted term at degree $n\geq1$ is $C_{ij}X_i^{n-1}/(n-1)!$, so no rearrangement of an infinite sum is needed.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivation only; agent-supplied formal coefficient argument: the explicit power induction giving the elementary commutation calculation

proof.text:
Let $P_j=E_1\cdots E_{j-1}$, including $P_1=1$. For fixed $j$, move $X_j$ through this prefix using step 4, beginning with $E_{j-1}X_j$. Each correction $C_{ij}$ commutes with every earlier $E_k$ by the hypothesis and the coefficient argument of step 1. Explicitly, if
$$E_m\cdots E_{j-1}X_j=(X_j+u\sum_{i=m}^{j-1}C_{ij})E_m\cdots E_{j-1},$$
left multiplication by $E_{m-1}$ and step 4 add exactly $uC_{m-1,j}$ to the sum. The base case is the empty suffix, where the sum is zero. Descending induction therefore gives
$$P_jX_j=(X_j+u\sum_{i<j}C_{ij})P_j.$$

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivation only; agent-supplied formal coefficient argument: the prefix induction, with its base case and the commuting correction terms

proof.text:
Set $F=E_1\cdots E_r$, with $F=1$ if $r=0$. Repeatedly apply the product rule of step 2 and $DE_j=X_jE_j$ from step 3. The summand where $E_j$ is differentiated is $P_jX_jE_j\cdots E_r$. Substitute step 5 into this summand and add over $j$:
$$DF=\sum_j(X_j+u\sum_{i<j}C_{ij})F=(S+uC)F.$$
The finite product rule itself follows by induction on $r$ from the two-factor rule, with $D1=0$. This also verifies the displayed formula at $r=0$, where $S=C=0$. Since every factor commutes with $C$, so does $F$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivation only; agent-supplied formal coefficient argument: differentiate the ordered product and identify the sign of the bracket sum

proof.text:
Put $H=FQ$. Using the two derivatives already computed and $FC=CF$, the product rule gives
$$DH=(S+uC)FQ-uFCQ=SH.$$
Also $H(0)=1$. Write $H=\sum h_nu^n$. Its differential equation is exactly $(n+1)h_{n+1}=Sh_n$ for $n\geq0$. Starting at $h_0=1$, induction and division by the nonzero rational integer $n+1$ give $h_n=S^n/n!$. This division is valid in every unital $\mathbf Q$-algebra; no integral-domain hypothesis is used. Consequently
$$E_S(u)=\bigl(E_1(u)\cdots E_r(u)\bigr)Q(u)\quad\text{in }B[[u]].$$

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), printed p.510, motivation only; agent-supplied formal coefficient argument: cancel the correction derivative and solve the explicit coefficient recurrence

proof.text: It remains to justify the specialization $u=1$ in this particular identity. A product of $n$ series in $(s,t)B$ has zero coefficient in every total degree less than $n$: in its Cauchy product every factor contributes positive total degree. Thus $X_i^n$ and $S^n$ have this bound, while $C^n$ has zero coefficients below total degree $2n$, since each $C_{ij}$ is a difference of products of two such series. For fixed $a,b\geq0$, taking the coefficient of $s^at^b$ in each of $E_i,E_S,Q$ therefore gives a polynomial in $u$ of degree at most $a+b$. The same holds for their finite products: split $(a,b)$ among the finitely many factors in the Cauchy formula, and add the respective bounds on the $u$ degrees. Hence step 7 gives an equality of polynomials in the central variable $u$ with coefficients in $A$, separately at every $(a,b)$. Evaluation at $u=1$ preserves finite sums and ordered products of these polynomials. The resulting coefficients are precisely those of $\exp(S)$, $\exp(X_i)$ and $\exp(-C/2)$, respectively, by their defining finite coefficient sums. Equality for every $(a,b)$ proves the formula in the item. When $r=0$ it reads $\exp(0)=1\cdot\exp(0)=1$, and when $r=1$ the correction is $1$.
